The [MoSCoW method](https://www.productplan.com/glossary/moscow-prioritization) is `a popular prioritization framework used in project management, software development, and business analysis to reach a consensus with stakeholders on the relative importance of requirements`.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MoSCoW_method)

### The MoSCoW Categories

The acronym stands for four distinct levels of priority, with lowercase "o"s added to make the word pronounceable:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MoSCoW_method)

- **M – Must have:** Non-negotiable, critical requirements that are mandatory for the project or release to be considered a success. If even one must-have is missing, the delivery fails.[[1]](https://community.atlassian.com/forums/discussion/2463999/understanding-the-moscow-prioritization-how-to-implement-it-into-your-project)[[2]](https://www.projectmanagement.com/wikis/483402/moscow-method)[[3]](https://www.techtarget.com/it-infrastructure/definition/MoSCoW-method)
- **S – Should have:** Important and high-priority items that add significant value, but are not strictly vital for immediate delivery . They can work via temporary workarounds if necessary.[[1]](https://www.agilebusiness.org/resource/what-is-moscow-prioritization/)[[2]](https://www.projectmanagement.com/wikis/483402/moscow-method)[[3]](https://productschool.com/blog/product-strategy/moscow-prioritization)
- **C – Could have:** Desirable, lower-impact enhancements or features that will be included only if time, budget, and resources permit.[[1]](https://www.agilebusiness.org/resource/what-is-moscow-prioritization/)[[2]](https://community.atlassian.com/forums/discussion/2463999/understanding-the-moscow-prioritization-how-to-implement-it-into-your-project)
- **W – Won't have (or Will not have this time):** Excluded requirements agreed upon by stakeholders to drop from the current timeframe, helping to prevent scope creep. They may be revisited in future cycles.[[1]](https://monday.com/blog/project-management/moscow-prioritization-method/)[[2]](https://www.agilebusiness.org/resource/what-is-moscow-prioritization/)[[3]](https://www.projectmanagement.com/wikis/483402/moscow-method)

### Best Practices

- **Cap Must-Haves:** Keep must-have items to roughly 60% or less of total available effort to ensure the project remains achievable.[[1]](https://www.agilebusiness.org/resource/what-is-moscow-prioritization/)[[2]](https://monday.com/blog/project-management/moscow-prioritization-method/)
- **Use Contingency:** Reserve about 20% of effort for could-have items or unexpected hurdles.[[1]](https://www.agilebusiness.org/resource/what-is-moscow-prioritization/)[[2]](https://monday.com/blog/project-management/moscow-prioritization-method/)
- **Prevent Scope Creep:** Leverage the "Won't have" category actively to set firm boundaries and manage stakeholder expectations early.[[1]](https://monday.com/blog/project-management/moscow-prioritization-method/)
